```{r setup}
library(omiprep)
```

## Who this vignette is for

`omiprep` ships dedicated readers for four commercial platforms — `read_metabolon()`,
`read_nightingale()`, `read_olink()` and `read_somalogic()`. Those readers exist only to
translate a vendor's particular spreadsheet layout into a common structure. They are a
convenience, **not** a requirement.

If your data were generated in-house, come from a platform without a dedicated reader, or
have already been through an upstream pipeline, you can build an `Omiprep` object directly
from flat text files. Everything downstream — `quality_control()`, `summarise()`,
`generate_report()`, `export()` — then behaves identically, because all the readers do is
produce the same three tables you will assemble here by hand.

## The three tables

An `Omiprep` object is built from exactly three pieces:

| Piece | Shape | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| `data` | numeric matrix, **samples in rows, features in columns** | `rownames` are sample ids, `colnames` are feature ids |
| `samples` | data.frame, one row per sample | must contain a column named `sample_id` |
| `features` | data.frame, one row per feature | must contain a column named `feature_id` |

Beyond those two id columns, both metadata tables are free-form: add as many annotation
columns as you like (batch, run order, sex, age, pathway, assay panel, LOD), or none at all.
`omiprep` carries them through QC and reporting untouched.

### Are the column names strict?

**Yes.** `sample_id` and `feature_id` are matched exactly and are **case-sensitive**. There is
no automatic mapping or fuzzy matching: `Sample_ID`, `sampleID` and `SampleId` are all
rejected, with an error naming the column it expected.

This is a deliberate design choice — silently guessing which of a user's columns holds the
identifier is a good way to mis-assign an entire dataset. Conforming is a one-line rename,
shown below.

## A worked example from flat text files

The package bundles a small example dataset as three plain CSV files, in exactly the form an
in-house pipeline might produce them.

```{r file_paths}
pkg <- "omiprep"
data_file     <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_data.csv",     package = pkg)
samples_file  <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_samples.csv",  package = pkg)
features_file <- system.file("extdata", "dummy_features.csv", package = pkg)
```

### 1) Read the measurement matrix

The measurement table has sample ids in the first column and feature ids as headers. Read it
with `row.names = 1` and coerce to a matrix. `check.names = FALSE` keeps feature ids exactly
as written — without it, R prefixes purely numeric column names with `X`.

```{r read_data}
data <- as.matrix(read.csv(data_file, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))

dim(data)
data[1:4, 1:3]
```

For a tab-delimited file, use `read.delim()` instead; nothing else changes.

### 2) Read the sample and feature metadata

```{r read_meta}
samples  <- read.csv(samples_file,  row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
features <- read.csv(features_file, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)

names(samples)
names(features)
```

Both tables already carry the required id columns alongside their annotation.

```{r show_meta}
head(samples[, c("sample_id", "sex", "age", "bmi")], 3)
head(features[, c("feature_id", "biochemical", "super_pathway")], 3)
```

### 3) Build the object

```{r build}
mydata <- Omiprep(data = data, samples = samples, features = features)

summary(mydata)
```

That is the whole import. From here the object is indistinguishable from one produced by
`read_metabolon()`.

## Renaming your own columns

If your files use different identifier names, rename them before constructing the object:

```{r rename_demo}
# a metadata table as an in-house pipeline might label it
inhouse <- data.frame(
  SampleName = samples$sample_id,
  RunBatch   = samples$`LC/MS Polar`
)

names(inhouse)[names(inhouse) == "SampleName"] <- "sample_id"
names(inhouse)
```

The helper `clean_names()` is useful when your headers contain spaces, dots, dashes or
percent signs. It lowercases and standardises them, which turns a header like `Sample ID`
into `sample_id` directly:

```{r clean_names_demo}
clean_names(c("Sample ID", "Feature-Name.1", "Concentration %"))
```

Note that `clean_names()` lowercases everything, so apply it to the whole header vector
rather than to one column, and check the result before relying on it.

## Identifier types: a common pitfall

Matrix `dimnames` in R are *always* character. If your ids are numeric and you read the
metadata without specifying types, `read.csv()` will type them as integer, and the ids will
not compare equal to the matrix names.

`Omiprep()` guards against this by coercing `sample_id` and `feature_id` to character for
you, so the naive read used above works. If you assemble metadata by some other route, it is
still worth being explicit:

```{r colclasses_demo, eval = FALSE}
features <- read.csv(features_file, colClasses = c(feature_id = "character"))
```

The ids must match the matrix names as a **set**; order does not matter. The constructor
reorders both metadata tables to follow the matrix, carrying all annotation columns with
them. Any id present in the matrix but absent from the metadata is an error, and the message
names the offending ids.

## A minimal object

Annotation is optional. If you have nothing but a matrix, generate the two id columns from
its dimnames:

```{r minimal}
minimal <- Omiprep(
  data     = data,
  samples  = data.frame(sample_id  = rownames(data)),
  features = data.frame(feature_id = colnames(data))
)

dim(minimal@data)
```

## Running the pipeline

Everything downstream now works as documented elsewhere. Quality control:

```{r qc, message = FALSE}
mydata <- quality_control(
  mydata,
  source_layer        = "input",
  sample_missingness  = 0.2,
  feature_missingness = 0.2,
  cores               = 2
)
```

```{r qc_summary}
summary(mydata)
```

Note that `total_sum_abundance_sd` assumes features share a comparable abundance scale. For
in-house data that has already been normalised, standardised, or combined across assays, set
it to `NA` to skip that step, as total abundance across such features is not interpretable.
